subject: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?

messages.author: 312c0b3a1aed795e
messages.subject: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
parts:
Dear All

Two questions, one practical the other more general. Both probably
demonstrate my inexperience with DISTANCE, in which case I apologise in
advance!

The first question:

I am interested in modelling bird count data (either from point or line
transects) using GLM (e.g. log-linear models with Poisson error term) to
assess the influence of various factors, covariates and their
interactions on the count. In the analysis I would like to take into
account differences in the detection probability (primarily arising from
habitat differences).

It strikes me I can use DISTANCE to calculate probabilities of detection
(by habitat if the sample size allows) and then adjust the raw data for
each count by this figure and then use this adjusted figure in the GLM.
However, if I do this the resulting adjusted density value for the
individual sample will not reflect the variation in the probability of
detection?

In answer to a similar question to this list: "Beyond z-tests" (Maddox,
6 Mar 2002). It seemed (to me!) to be suggested that a weighing vector
could be include to reflect the variation in the detection probability
between habitats and this included in the GLM (presumably with the same
weighting vector value used for all counts in a particular habitat?). Is
this appropriate? What method could I use to identify whether the
detection function in fact varies between habitats (comparing AICs of
various runs pooling the data differently by habitats until I get the
lowest values?).

In answers to this question: "Adjusting counts for detectability and
covariates" (Tucker, 11 May 2004). Another way was suggested, I quote:

"I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but
with
habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the
probability
of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the point and that
the
animal is present within the truncation distance. You then want to
calculate
density (or abundance) at each point using this habitat-specific
probability of
detection.
You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the
Model
Definition | Estimate tab. Under "Quantities to estimate and level of
resolution", for the Density and the detection function rows, tick both
the
"Global" and "Sample" columns. Make sure you have habitat as a
covariate. For
more about this, see the online help, Chapter 9, Defining MCDS models,
Estimating the detection function at multiple levels.
The output you will get will be density for each point, and p_i for
animals at
each point too. (You will also get abundance for each point, but
there's a bug
in Distance where the area used to calculate this is currently wrong so
it's
acutally abunance for the whole study area assuming density at that
point
applies to the whole study area -- this bug is fixed in the next version
of
Distance to be released.)"

If the output I get is "density for each point, and p_i for animals at
each point too" then I could use the "p_i" as the weighting vector?? Is
this a better (different?) or more appropriate way?


Second question (sorry, its very basic compared to the first).

I currently work in conservation in Indonesia and I regularly see
DISTANCE used as a simple recipe for calculating absolute densities,
typically using all default values in the programme (against all
advice!), and without any great understanding of what AICs, CVs, CIs etc
actually mean.

Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated
density but this is regularly justified by saying that "the 'real' value
must be within the confidence intervals somewhere". What is the simple
answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will
give you little information on density, or that a CV of over 20%
suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
density estimate outright?


Yours

Nick Brickle
ni...@brickle.com
Bogor, Indonesia.

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
parts:
Hi Nick, list,

What you're proposing is what we sometimes call "spatial modelling" or
"spatial density surface estimation". I'll attempt an answer, but I'm no
expert so others may want to contribute more. Also, there's some stuff on
this in Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book.

To begin with, you need to do the detection function modelling in Distance.
You could either stratify by habitat, or put habitat in as a factor
covariate in the MCDS engine. If you have enough data, and no problems such
as avoidance, rounding, etc, then you could try both and let AIC tell you
which is better. If using MCDS then you could include other covariates too.
Once you've finished this modelling, you want an estimate of detection
probabilty by point (p_k) (Note, I'm omiting hats from estimates to avoid
cumbersome text notation. Also, for now, I'm assuming you don't have any
species level covariates such as cluster size). To do this, you ask for
density by sample, as in my reply to "Adjusting counts for detectability

Now you need to incorporate the estimates of p_k into the spatial model for
the bird counts. To my knowledge there are three ways to do this:

1. Divide the observed count at each point n_k by the estimated p_k to get
an estimate of abundance at each point N_k. This abundance is non-integer,
so:
2. you might want to divide N_k by the area of each point (pi*w^2) to get an
estimated density at each point D_k. Doesn't make much difference really.
Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson error term as the
response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?
3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use
pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius for
that point.

Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the counts.
However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level covariates, such
as sex of bird or cluster size. In that case, you don't know what the
effective detection radius is when you observe no birds -- but you do know
that the estiamate of density is 0. If you have species level covariates in
1 or 2 you estimate N_k by the sum of 1/p_i for each bird i detected at the
point. There is a section of the online manual that says how to calculate
p_i for each animal given the parameter estiamtes of the detection function.

In practice, two problems usually present themselves:

1. Overdispersion. Often many points have 0 birds seen, so you get data
with lots of zeros and relatively few high counts (or high D_ks if the p_ks
are sometimes small). Can be hard to model. Can perhaps investigate the
various zero-inflated models that are out there?

2. Variance estimation. How does one incorporate the variance due to
estimating the detection function in the final variance estiamte from the
spatial model? An easy way is a nonparametric bootstrap or jacknife of
points, but you need plenty of points for this. Various parametric
bootstraps have been proposed - I think there is something on this in
Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book. It may be possible to do
something analytic based on the delta method -- don't know.

So, hope this helps -- as I said others may be able to contribute more.
I'll answer your second question in a separate email.

Cheers,

- Len

messages.subject: Re: Detection adjustment prior to GLM of count data?
parts:
> >Second question (sorry, its very basic compared to the first).

> >I currently work in conservation in Indonesia and I regularly see
> >DISTANCE used as a simple recipe for calculating absolute densities,
> >typically using all default values in the programme (against all
> >advice!), and without any great understanding of what AICs, CVs, CIs etc
> >actually mean.

Argh! Hopefully you can do your bit in training people to make intellegent
use of the program. Also, I've found in general that people who have a poor
understanding of the program options also have a poor understanding of how
to design surveys and implement field methods that give reliable results.
Just my prejudice I guess.

> >Very small sample sizes often lead to very high variation in estimated
> >density but this is regularly justified by saying that "the 'real' value
> >must be within the confidence intervals somewhere". What is the simple
> >answer to this question? I can tell people that a sample size of 10 will
> >give you little information on density, or that a CV of over 20%
> >suggests a pretty inaccurate estimate, but by that point most people
> >already have a figure for density on the print-out and they are happy!
> >My question: What combination of criteria would lead you to reject a
> >density estimate outright?

I'm afraid it's not that simple. Getting a reliable estimate requires more
than just an "adequate" sample size of observations, and the required sample
size depends on factors such as the type of survey (points require more than
lines), and shape of the detection function (wide shoulders require fewer
observations to accurately model). Also, remember that you also need a
"decent" sample size of lines or points for reliable estimation of the
encounter rate variance.

Here's a very rough checklist for initial assessment of a study:

- were the lines/points laid out according to a randomized survey design?
Ideally there should be 20 or more lines or points - many fewer than that
and I'd doubt the encounter rate variance estiamtes. If the analysis is
stratified, you'd like 20 lines per stratum if possible.

- is g(0) likely to be 1?

- is animal movement likely to be a problem? (is there evasive movement, or
do animals move at more than 1/3-half the speed of the observer for line
transects; were the point transects performed over a "long" time period (ie
not a snapshot))

- were distances measured accurately?

- does the detection function have a wide shoulder?

- is the sample size of observations reasonable? (60-80 recommended,
although for wide shoulders and line transects can get away with far fewer).
If the detection function is estimated by stratum, you'd like 60-80
observations by stratum if possible.

- does the analysis look like it was performed competently?

- do the reported results give both the estimate and CI/CV, and
interpretation of the results take account of the uncertainty in the
estimate.

I've probably forgotten something, but hope this helps. Perhaps someone
else will be willing to stick their neck out and offer more absolute rules
of thumb!

- Len
